concept.name: Null hypothesis
concept.definition: The default statement in a hypothesis test that there is no effect or no difference - the status quo that sample evidence must argue against. It always contains a statement of equality (e.g., mu = mu_0) and is the claim that is rejected or not rejected, never 'proven'.
concept.intuition: It is the skeptical position: 'this strategy has no edge, the apparent performance is luck.' Testing asks whether the data are surprising enough under that assumption to abandon it.
concept.mechanics: The null specifies a parameter value or distribution (e.g., H0: mu = mu_0). A test statistic is computed from the sample, and if its value falls in the critical region defined by the significance level alpha, H0 is rejected in favor of the alternative; otherwise the conclusion is 'do not reject', not 'accept'.
concept.formula: Typical form: H0: mu = mu_0 (or H0: p <= p_0), versus the alternative Ha: mu != mu_0 (or p > p_0); test statistic for a mean: T = (Y_bar - mu_0) / (s/sqrt(N)).
concept.failure_modes: Failing to reject H0 does not establish it as true - an underpowered test on few trades will fail to reject almost any null. The framework also only evaluates the stated null, so a misspecified model (wrong distribution, ignored costs) makes rejection or non-rejection meaningless.
concept.misconceptions: One never 'accepts the null hypothesis'; absence of evidence against H0 is not evidence for it. Also, the null need not be 'zero effect' in every application - it is whatever default statement the analyst sets up to test.
concept.example: Testing a trading signal, H0: mean daily excess return = 0; with T = 2.8 exceeding the 5% critical value 1.97, the null of no edge is rejected - though this says nothing about whether the edge covers transaction costs.
